idiom_name: std::ranges::fold_left / fold_right (C++23) or std::accumulate over a range
implementation_notes: The sequence fold is in the standard library: since C++23 <algorithm> carries the fold family (std::ranges::fold_left, fold_left_first, fold_right, fold_right_last, plus the _with_iter forms that report how far the range was consumed) and <numeric> has always carried std::accumulate, whose specification is literally acc = op(std::move(acc), *i) in order - a left fold with the move in C++20 and later. Use the ranges spellings when the carrier is a range and the operation is a function object; use accumulate on C++20 toolchains (feature-test with __cpp_lib_ranges_fold), and remember that accumulate's in-order definition makes it correct for non-associative operations while std::reduce is not. A recursive data type still needs the variant over std::variant, because the standard library has no catamorphism for user types.
pitfalls: fold_left is C++23 while ranges themselves are C++20: guard with the __cpp_lib_ranges_fold feature-test macro (or fall back to std::accumulate over the view's iterators) instead of assuming the fold family exists wherever concepts do.

std::accumulate and std::reduce look interchangeable and are not: accumulate folds in order, reduce may permute and aggregate in unspecified manner, so only an associative (and commutative) op belongs in reduce.

A ranges fold cannot short-circuit: the first failure or first match needs ranges::find/any_of or a std::optional/std::expected carrier that carries the stop, otherwise the fold shape has to be abandoned for a hand-written loop.

variants.name: Hand-written catamorphism over a std::variant node type
variants.idiom_name: std::variant cases + recursive fold dispatched by std::visit over an overload set
variants.implementation_notes: The structural form in modern C++: model the cases as a std::variant of case types (with std::unique_ptr or std::vector at the recursive positions), write the algebra as one overload set over the alternatives, and let a recursive function apply std::visit to the folded children - std::visit applies the visitor to the alternative actually held, so the visitor is the case combiner and the alternative list makes a missing case a compile error, which the classic OO Visitor only gets by remembering to write an accept per node. This is the variant to pick when the data really is a sum of cases (AST, protocol message, document node); for a homogeneous sequence the ranges fold is shorter and better optimised.
pitfalls: A std::variant cannot hold itself, so every recursive position needs indirection (unique_ptr/shared_ptr or a container) and the node type becomes heap-shaped: the fold allocates per node, and a shared_ptr used where unique_ptr would do hides the ownership question the fold depends on.

std::visit requires the visitor to handle every alternative: that is the compile-time exhaustiveness check, but the diagnostic names the visitor rather than the missing case, and an overload set that silently accepts convertible types can make an unrelated alternative match the wrong lambda.
Recursion depth is tree depth with no portable tail-call guarantee: the fold combines two children before returning, so deeply nested input overflows the stack and needs an explicit worklist.

variants.name: Parallel reduce with an execution policy (std::reduce)
variants.implementation_notes: std::reduce (C++17, <numeric>) is the fold that may be executed out of order: with an execution policy the range is "possibly permuted and aggregated in unspecified manner", which is why the operation must be associative and commutative and why a floating-point reduce does not reproduce the serial accumulate's value. Use it for large input and a genuine monoid over an associative, commutative operation (sums, counts, max, bitwise maps); keep accumulate/fold_left for order-sensitive combines. Whole-program parallel execution is only an option: whether a policy is backed by a parallel implementation depends on the toolchain (for example a TBB-backed std::execution), and a build without one may silently run the algorithm serially.
pitfalls: A non-commutative or non-associative op (subtraction, concatenation, averaging) produces a different result per partition, and neither the compiler nor the standard library can detect it - the algebra's laws are the user's obligation.
Neither the order nor the number of invocations of op is specified, so an op that mutates shared state, logs, or counts its calls is undefined behaviour rather than merely slow.

The parallel backend is not guaranteed to exist: without a parallel implementation linked in, std::reduce with std::execution::par may execute serially, so timing must never be treated as a correctness or performance proof.
